fact: Selectins mediate the first, low-affinity adhesion of circulating leukocytes to endothelial cells of postcapillary venules.
quote: Selectins are plasma membrane carbohydrate-binding adhesion molecules that mediate an initial step of low-affinity adhesion of circulating leukocytes

fact: Endothelial cells express P-selectin (CD62P) and E-selectin (CD62E).
quote: Endothelial cells express two types of selectins, called P-selectin (CD62P) and E-selectin (CD62E).

fact: Leukocytes, not endothelial cells, express L-selectin (CD62L).
quote: A third selectin, called L-selectin (CD62L), is expressed on leukocytes and not on endothelial cells.

fact: P-selectin is stored in endothelial granules and moves rapidly to the luminal surface in response to histamine and thrombin.
quote: is stored in cytoplasmic granules of endothelial cells and is rapidly redistributed to the luminal surface in response to histamine from mast cells

fact: IL-1 and TNF induce E-selectin expression on endothelial cells within 1 to 2 hours.
quote: E-selectin is synthesized and expressed on the endothelial cell surface within 1 to 2 hours in response to the cytokines interleukin-1 (IL-1)

fact: The best-defined leukocyte ligand for E-selectin and P-selectin is the tetrasaccharide sialyl Lewis X.
quote: The best defined of these is the tetrasaccharide sialyl Lewis X

fact: PSGL-1 on leukocytes displays sialyl Lewis X, the major carbohydrate ligand for P-selectin.
quote: P-selectin glycoprotein ligand 1 (PSGL-1) is posttranslationally modified to display sialyl Lewis X, which serves as the major carbohydrate ligand for P-selectin

fact: Endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies contain preformed P-selectin.
quote: induce the rapid externalization of granules called Weibel-Palade bodies in the endothelial cells. These granules contain preformed P-selectin

fact: Selectin-ligand bonds have low affinity and a fast off-rate, so they form and break repeatedly and the leukocyte rolls.
quote: the interactions of selectins with their ligands are of low affinity (Kd ~100 μm) with a fast off-rate

fact: Integrins are heterodimers of one alpha chain and one beta chain.
quote: all of which are heterodimers containing 1 of 18 types of α chains and 1 of 8 types of β chains

fact: LFA-1 (CD11aCD18) binds ICAM-1 (CD54) on cytokine-activated endothelium.
quote: One important ligand for LFA-1 is intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1, CD54), a membrane glycoprotein expressed on cytokine-activated endothelial cells

fact: MAC-1 (CD11bCD18) is also complement receptor 3 (CR3); it binds ICAM-1 and iC3b-opsonized particles.
quote: MAC-1 (αMβ2, CD11bCD18, or complement receptor 3 [CR3]) on circulating monocytes binds to ICAM-1 and mediates adhesion to endothelium

fact: VLA-4 binds VCAM-1 (CD106) on cytokine-activated endothelium.
quote: VLA-4 binds to vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (VCAM-1, CD106), an Ig superfamily protein expressed on cytokine-activated endothelial cells

fact: Chemokine receptor signals change integrin conformation to a high-affinity state; this is called inside-out signalling.
quote: alter the binding functions of the extracellular domain of integrins is called inside-out signaling

fact: Endothelial heparan sulfate proteoglycans bind chemokines and display them to adherent leukocytes.
quote: Chemokines produced in the tissues bind to heparan sulfate proteoglycans on endothelial cells that line postcapillary venules

fact: Leukocyte recruitment follows selectin-mediated rolling, chemokine-mediated integrin activation, stable integrin-mediated arrest and transmigration.
quote: Selectin-mediated rolling of leukocytes on endothelium... Chemokine-mediated increase in affinity of integrins... Stable integrin-mediated arrest... Transmigration of leukocytes through the endothelium

fact: For firm arrest, cytokines upregulate endothelial VCAM-1 (binds VLA-4) and ICAM-1 (binds LFA-1 and MAC-1).
quote: These ligands include VCAM-1, which binds the integrin VLA-4, and ICAM-1, which binds LFA-1 and MAC-1 integrins

fact: Leukocytes usually migrate between endothelial cells; Abbas calls this paracellular transmigration or diapedesis.
quote: Leukocytes usually migrate out of blood vessels between endothelial cells, a process called paracellular transmigration or diapedesis

fact: Transmigration involves CD31 and a reversible disruption of the VE-cadherin junction complex.
quote: notably CD31... This process requires a transient and reversible disruption of adherens junction proteins, primarily the VE-cadherin complex

fact: Janeway uses the term diapedesis for the movement through the basement membrane, after the cell squeezes between endothelial cells using PECAM (CD31).
quote: The movement through the basement membrane is known as diapedesis, and it enables phagocytes to enter the subendothelial tissues.

fact: Chemotaxis is movement of cells along a chemoattractant concentration gradient toward its source.
quote: Chemokines stimulate movement of cells along the concentration gradient of the secreted proteins toward their source, a process called chemotaxis

fact: CXC chemokines with an ELR motif support neutrophil migration.
quote: CXC chemokines with ELR motifs support neutrophil migration.

fact: Chemokine receptors are seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
quote: The receptors for chemokines belong to the seven-transmembrane, guanosine triphosphate-binding (G) protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) superfamily.

fact: Neutrophils express CXCR1 and CXCR2, which bind CXCL1 and CXCL8 (IL-8).
quote: Neutrophils express CXCR1 and CXCR2, which bind CXCL1 and CXCL8 (IL-8), the major chemokines with ELR motifs

fact: Classical monocytes express CCR2; its most important ligand for monocyte recruitment is CCL2 (MCP-1).
quote: classical monocytes... express CCR2. This receptor binds several chemokines, the most important one for monocyte recruitment being CCL2 (MCP-1)

fact: C5a, C3a and leukotriene B4 (LTB4) are chemoattractants for phagocytes and act through GPCRs.
quote: The C3a and C5a complement fragments... and the arachidonic acid metabolite leukotriene B4 (LTB4) are important chemoattractants that promote phagocyte migration

fact: Formyl peptide receptor 1 (FPR1) recognizes N-formylmethionyl bacterial peptides, which are among the most potent leukocyte chemoattractants.
quote: The bacterial peptide ligands that bind this receptor are some of the most potent known chemoattractants for leukocytes.

fact: The fMLP receptor is a GPCR; its signals direct cell movement and induce reactive oxygen species in the phagolysosome.
quote: Signaling through the fMLP receptor also induces the production of microbicidal reactive oxygen species in the phagolysosome.

fact: Neutrophils exposed to C5a or CXCL8 are activated to produce the respiratory burst.
quote: neutrophils exposed to C5a or CXCL8 are activated to produce the respiratory burst that generates oxygen radicals and nitric oxide

fact: Neutrophils are usually the most numerous leukocytes in tissue within 24 to 48 hours of infection and are then replaced by monocytes.
quote: neutrophils are usually the most numerous type of leukocyte to accumulate in tissues, within 24 to 48 hours after the onset of an infection

fact: Janeway states that neutrophil influx usually peaks within the first 6 hours of an inflammatory response.
quote: Their influx usually peaks within the first 6 hours of an inflammatory response, whereas monocytes can be recruited later, through the action of CCL2.

fact: An adult makes more than 1 x 10^11 neutrophils per day; each circulates from a few hours to up to 5 days.
quote: produces more than 1 × 10^11 neutrophils per day, each of which circulates in the blood from a few hours to up to 5 days

fact: Neutrophil life span in tissues is 1 to 2 days; tissue-resident macrophages can live for years.
quote: Life span in tissues 1–2 days ... Tissue-resident macrophages: years

fact: Neutrophil production is stimulated by G-CSF and GM-CSF.
quote: Production of neutrophils is stimulated by granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).

fact: Neutrophil specific granules contain lysozyme, collagenase and elastase; azurophilic granules contain myeloperoxidase, defensins and cathelicidins.
quote: specific granules, are filled with enzymes, such as lysozyme, collagenase, and elastase... azurophilic granules... contain enzymes (e.g., myeloperoxidase)

fact: Dead and dying neutrophils are a major component of pus.
quote: Dead and dying neutrophils are a major component of the pus that forms in abscesses

fact: Phagocytosis is an active, energy-dependent engulfment of particles larger than 0.5 micrometre.
quote: Phagocytosis is an active, energy-dependent process of engulfment of large particles (greater than 0.5 μm in diameter) into vesicles.

fact: Binding of the microbe to phagocyte receptors is the first step of phagocytosis; some are PRRs such as C-type lectins and scavenger receptors.
quote: binding of microbes to these receptors is the first step in phagocytosis... pattern recognition receptors, including C-type lectins and scavenger receptors

fact: Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen with antibodies and/or complement proteins so that phagocytes take it up more readily.
quote: Opsonization refers to the coating of a pathogen by antibodies and/or complement proteins so that it is more readily taken up

fact: FcγRI (CD64) is a high-affinity IgG receptor on macrophages and neutrophils; it binds IgG1 and IgG3 and mediates phagocytosis.
quote: FcγRI (CD64) High (Kd ~10−9 M); binds IgG1 and IgG3, can bind monomeric IgG ... Phagocytosis; activation of phagocytes

fact: CR1 (CD35) is a high-affinity receptor for C3b and C4b; phagocytes use it to bind and internalize opsonized particles.
quote: CR1 is a high-affinity receptor for C3b and C4b... Phagocytes use this receptor to bind and internalize particles opsonized with C3b or C4b.

fact: CR1 alone is inefficient at inducing phagocytosis; simultaneous IgG-FcγR binding or IFN-γ activation enhances it.
quote: By itself, CR1 is inefficient at inducing the phagocytosis of C3b-coated microbes, but its ability to do so is enhanced

fact: C5a can activate macrophages to ingest bacteria bound to CR1.
quote: the small complement fragment C5a can activate macrophages to ingest bacteria bound to their CR1 receptors

fact: CR3 (MAC-1, CD11bCD18) is an integrin receptor for iC3b; its beta chain CD18 is shared with LFA-1 and CR4.
quote: The type 3 complement receptor, also called MAC-1 (CR3, CD11bCD18), is an integrin that functions as a receptor for the iC3b fragment

fact: CR3 also directly recognizes and phagocytoses microbes that bear beta-glucans.
quote: The complement receptor CR3 also directly recognizes and phagocytoses microbes bearing B-glucans.

fact: The membrane cup closes around the particle to form a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome.
quote: the top of the cup closes over and pinches off the interior of the cup to form an inside-out intracellular vesicle

fact: Fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes forms phagolysosomes, where most microbicidal mechanisms are concentrated.
quote: The fusion of phagocytic vacuoles (phagosomes) with lysosomes results in the formation of phagolysosomes, where most of the microbicidal mechanisms are concentrated.

fact: Signals from TLRs, Fc and C3b receptors, IFN-γ receptors and CD40 activate phagocytes to kill ingested microbes.
quote: pattern recognition receptors (such as TLRs), opsonin receptors (such as Fc and C3b receptors), receptors for cytokines (mainly IFN-γ), and CD40

fact: The three most important classes of microbicidal molecules are reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide and proteolytic enzymes.
quote: Three classes of microbicidal molecules are known to be the most important.

fact: Phagocyte (NADPH) oxidase is a multisubunit enzyme assembled mainly in the phagolysosomal membrane of activated phagocytes.
quote: Phagocyte oxidase is a multisubunit enzyme that is assembled in activated phagocytes, mainly in the phagolysosomal membrane.

fact: Phagocyte oxidase reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide, with NADPH as cofactor.
quote: to chemically reduce molecular oxygen into ROS, such as superoxide radicals, with the reduced form of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) acting as a cofactor

fact: Superoxide is dismutated to hydrogen peroxide; myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide to convert halide ions into toxic hypohalous acids.
quote: Superoxide is enzymatically dismutated into hydrogen peroxide, which is used by the enzyme myeloperoxidase to convert normally unreactive halide ions into reactive hypohalous acids

fact: The process is called the respiratory burst because it requires oxygen consumption.
quote: The process by which ROS are produced is called the respiratory burst because it requires oxygen consumption

fact: Cytochrome b558 subunits (gp91 and p22) sit in secondary granule membranes; p40, p47 and p67 are cytosolic in resting neutrophils.
quote: subunits (gp91 and gp22) of the NADPH oxidase are localized in the membranes of secondary granules; the other oxidase components (p40, p47, and p67)

fact: fMLP and C5a receptor signals activate Rac2, which is needed for NADPH oxidase assembly.
quote: activating Ras-family GTPases, such as Rac2, that are necessary for the assembly of the active NADPH oxidase

fact: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; further reactions produce hypochlorite and hydroxyl radical.
quote: O2- is converted by superoxide dismutase (SOD) to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)... to microbicidal hypochlorite (OCl-) and the hydroxyl (•OH) radical

fact: Potassium and hydrogen ions enter the phagolysosome after superoxide forms; this releases and activates granule enzymes such as cathepsin G and elastase.
quote: Potassium and hydrogen ions are then drawn into the phagolysosome... Acidification dissociates granule enzymes such as cathepsin G and elastase

fact: Janeway notes that ROS alone may not kill; ROS-driven K+ influx raises vacuole pH to the optimum for microbicidal proteins.
quote: ROS cause an influx of K+ ions into the phagocytic vacuole, increasing the pH to the optimal level for the action of microbicidal peptides

fact: Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is absent in resting macrophages and is induced by TLR signals, especially with IFN-γ.
quote: absent in resting macrophages but is induced in response to microbial products that activate TLRs, especially in combination with IFN-γ

fact: iNOS converts arginine to citrulline and releases NO; NO combines with H2O2 or superoxide to form peroxynitrite.
quote: iNOS catalyzes the conversion of arginine to citrulline and freely diffusible NO gas is released... to produce highly reactive peroxynitrite radicals

fact: Neutrophils make low or no nitric oxide; macrophages make it after iNOS induction.
quote: Nitric oxide Low levels or none Induced after transcriptional activation of iNOS

fact: Elastase and cathepsin G are important neutrophil proteolytic enzymes for bacterial killing.
quote: One of the important enzymes in neutrophils is elastase, a broad-spectrum serine protease... Another important enzyme is cathepsin G.

fact: Defensins are cationic peptides made by epithelia and by neutrophils; they kill microbes mainly by disrupting microbial membranes.
quote: Defensins are produced by epithelial cells of mucosal surfaces and by granule-containing leukocytes, including neutrophils

fact: Neutrophil alpha-defensins are stored in primary granules, which fuse with phagosomes.
quote: generating a mature cationic defensin that is stored in the so-called primary granules

fact: Lysozyme digests cell walls of some Gram-positive bacteria; lactoferrin sequesters iron.
quote: Lysozyme: digests cell walls of some Gram-positive bacteria ... Lactoferrin (sequesters Fe2+)

fact: NETs are extruded DNA and histone strands with bound granule proteins (lysozyme, elastase, defensins) that trap and kill bacteria and fungi.
quote: are composed of strands of DNA and histones to which high concentrations of antimicrobial granule contents are bound, including lysozyme, elastase, and defensins

fact: NET formation needs PAD4-mediated histone citrullination, elastase, myeloperoxidase and phagocyte oxidase.
quote: NET formation requires citrullination of histones by the enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD4), as well as neutrophil serine protease elastase, myeloperoxidase, and phagocyte oxidase

fact: NET extrusion usually causes neutrophil death (NETosis); excessive NET formation contributes to autoimmune and inflammatory disease.
quote: usually leads to neutrophil cell death, referred to as NETosis... excessive NET formation contributes to autoimmune and other inflammatory diseases

fact: Phagocyte defects cause invasive bacterial or fungal infections of skin, liver and respiratory tract, mainly Aspergillus and Candida for fungi.
quote: invasive infections of the skin, liver, and respiratory tract with bacteria or fungi, the latter predominantly involving Aspergillus and Candida species

fact: Janeway groups phagocyte defects into defects of production, adhesion, activation and killing.
quote: deficiencies in phagocyte production, phagocyte adhesion, phagocyte activation, and phagocyte killing of microorganisms

fact: Flow cytometry can detect absence of a cell-surface or intracellular protein in immunodeficiency work-up.
quote: flow cytometric analysis of immune cells to evaluate numbers and relative proportions of these cells or the absence of a cell surface or intracellular protein

fact: CGD is caused by mutations in components of NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase).
quote: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is caused by mutations in components of the NADPH oxidase (also called phagocyte oxidase) enzyme complex.

fact: About two-thirds of CGD cases are X-linked recessive (gp91, the 91-kD subunit of cytochrome b558); the rest are autosomal recessive.
quote: Approximately two-thirds of cases show an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance, and the remainder are autosomal recessive.

fact: CGD affects about 1 in 200,000 individuals in the United States.
quote: estimated to affect approximately 1 in 200,000 individuals in the United States

fact: Autosomal recessive CGD (other oxidase subunits) can be milder, with later onset.
quote: Autosomal mutations in other subunits of the NADPH oxidase can also cause chronic granulomatous disease, but can be milder and have a later onset.

fact: Invasive Aspergillus infection is the leading cause of death in CGD.
quote: Invasive infection with the fungus Aspergillus is the leading cause of death.

fact: Catalase-producing organisms such as Staphylococcus are troublesome in CGD because catalase destroys the hydrogen peroxide from residual host superoxide.
quote: such as Staphylococcus, produce catalase, which destroys the microbicidal hydrogen peroxide that may be produced by host cells from residual superoxide

fact: In CGD, uncontrolled infection drives T cell-mediated macrophage activation and granuloma formation.
quote: they stimulate chronic cell-mediated immune responses, resulting in T cell-mediated macrophage activation and the formation of granulomas

fact: CGD management includes antibiotic and antifungal prophylaxis, IFN-γ, and consideration of HSCT; gene therapy trials are ongoing.
quote: Treatment with the cytokine IFN-γ can be used in addition to preventive antibiotic and antifungal therapy... standard of care to consider hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

fact: After HSCT, restoring neutrophil superoxide production to at least 15% of normal greatly improves resistance to infection.
quote: If neutrophil superoxide production is restored to at least 15% of normal levels after HSCT, resistance to infection is greatly improved.

fact: Secondary HLH can complicate CGD.
quote: Secondary HLH can also be seen as a complication of CGD

fact: Myeloperoxidase deficiency impairs intracellular killing and gives a CGD-like but less severe phenotype.
quote: Deficiencies in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and myeloperoxidase also impair intracellular bacterial killing and lead to a similar, although less severe, phenotype.

fact: Janeway lists G6PD deficiency and myeloperoxidase deficiency, with CGD, as defects of the respiratory burst.
quote: The respiratory burst is defective in chronic granulomatous disease, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, and myeloperoxidase deficiency.

fact: LADs are autosomal recessive; they cause failure of neutrophil recruitment, severe early bacterial infections and inability to make pus.
quote: The leukocyte adhesion deficiencies are a group of autosomal recessive disorders... severe bacterial infections starting early in life, and an inability to make pus

fact: LAD-1 is caused by CD18 mutations with absent or reduced beta2 integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, p150,95).
quote: absent or reduced expression of the β2 integrins... as a result of mutations in the CD18 gene

fact: LAD-1 causes recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, impaired wound healing and common leukocytosis.
quote: characterized by recurrent bacterial and fungal infections and impaired wound healing. Leukocytosis is common

fact: In LAD-1, adherence, aggregation, chemotaxis, phagocytosis and cytotoxicity of leukocytes are defective.
quote: including adherence to endothelium, neutrophil aggregation and chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and cytotoxicity mediated by neutrophils, NK cells, and T lymphocytes

fact: LAD-2 is caused by a defective GDP-fucose transporter; sialyl Lewis X is absent and leukocytes do not roll.
quote: caused by a mutation in a guanosine diphosphate (GDP)-fucose transporter... the absence of leukocyte rolling

fact: LAD-2 also causes severe developmental abnormalities and the Bombay blood group phenotype; it is a congenital disorder of glycosylation.
quote: This abnormality in fucosylation seen in LAD-2 also contributes to a Bombay blood group phenotype

fact: LAD-3 is caused mainly by KINDLIN-3 mutations that block inside-out chemokine-induced integrin activation.
quote: This deficiency is caused by a defect in the inside-out signaling pathway that mediates chemokine-induced integrin activation

fact: LAD-3 causes a life-threatening bleeding disorder from defective platelet aggregation, with normal platelet counts.
quote: a life-threatening bleeding disorder that requires blood transfusions because of defective platelet aggregation, even though blood platelet counts are normal

fact: Infections in LAD resist antibiotic treatment and show impaired wound healing and no pus.
quote: impaired wound healing and, in pyogenic bacterial infections, the absence of pus formation. The infections that occur in these patients are resistant to antibiotic treatment

fact: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (CHS) is autosomal recessive with pyogenic infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism and giant lysosomes in leukocytes.
quote: recurrent infections by pyogenic bacteria, partial oculocutaneous albinism... The neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes of these patients contain giant lysosomes.

fact: CHS is caused by mutations in LYST, which regulates intracellular trafficking of lysosomes.
quote: caused by mutations in the gene encoding the protein LYST, which regulates intracellular trafficking of lysosomes

fact: In CHS, NK cell function is impaired and leukocytes show defective chemotaxis and phagocytosis.
quote: NK cell function in these patients is impaired... Leukocytes are also defective in chemotaxis and phagocytosis

fact: Untransplanted CHS patients usually develop hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with fever, DIC, organomegaly and hemophagocytosis.
quote: CHS patients who are not transplanted will likely develop a life-threatening syndrome that includes fever, disseminated intravascular coagulation

fact: In CHS, phagosomes and lysosomes fail to fuse properly; phagocytes have enlarged granules and poor intracellular killing.
quote: causes a failure of lysosomes and phagosomes to fuse properly; the phagocytes in these patients have enlarged granules and impaired intracellular killing ability

fact: CHS features metallic silver hair, poor vision and platelet dysfunction with bleeding.
quote: The hair is typically a metallic silver color, vision is poor because of abnormalities in retinal pigment cells, and platelet dysfunction causes increased bleeding.

fact: Severe congenital neutropenia (SCN, Kostmann disease) has a persistent neutrophil count below 0.5 x 10^9/L.
quote: the neutrophil count is persistently less than 0.5 x 10^9 per liter of blood

fact: Cyclic neutropenia has neutrophil counts that fluctuate with a cycle of about 21 days.
quote: neutrophil numbers that fluctuate from near normal to very low or undetectable, with an approximate cycle time of 21 days

fact: Mutations in ELA2 (neutrophil elastase) are the most common cause of SCN; some ELA2 mutations cause cyclic neutropenia.
quote: sporadic or autosomal dominant mutations of the gene that encodes neutrophil elastase (ELA2)... Some mutations of ELA2 cause cyclic neutropenia

fact: HAX1 deficiency causes an autosomal recessive form of SCN.
quote: Autosomal recessive forms of SCN have also been identified. Deficiency of the mitochondrial protein HAX1 leads to increased apoptosis

fact: SCN and cyclic neutropenia carry an increased risk of myelodysplasia or myeloid leukemia; G-CSF is the mainstay of treatment.
quote: increased risk of developing myelodysplasia or myeloid leukemia... G-CSF which is now the mainstay of treatment for congenital neutropenias

fact: MSMD is severe disease from weakly virulent mycobacteria and other intracellular pathogens such as Salmonella; BCG vaccine can disseminate.
quote: predisposed to severe disease caused by weakly virulent mycobacteria that do not cause disease in healthy individuals... the vaccine can cause disseminated mycobacterial infection

fact: MSMD genes include IL-12p40, IL-12Rbeta1, both IFN-γ receptor chains, STAT1 and NEMO (IKKγ).
quote: Mutations in the genes encoding IL-12p40, the IL-12Rβ1 chain, and both chains of the IFN-γ receptor, as well as some mutations in STAT1 and IKKγ

fact: IL-12 from DCs and macrophages drives IFN-γ production by T cells and NK cells.
quote: IL-12R signaling stimulates the synthesis of IFN-γ by helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells

fact: Because p40 is shared by IL-12 and IL-23, p40 deficiency causes both IL-12 and IL-23 deficiency.
quote: p40 is shared by IL-12 and IL-23, and so p40 deficiency can cause both IL-12 and IL-23 deficiency.

fact: Total absence of IFN-γ receptor expression markedly reduces granuloma formation.
quote: In the total absence of IFN-y receptor expression, granuloma formation is much reduced

fact: MyD88 or IRAK4 deficiency causes severe pyogenic infections with little inflammation ('cold' infections).
quote: recurrent, severe peripheral, and invasive infections by pyogenic bacteria that elicit little inflammation, a situation known as a 'cold' infection

fact: Genetic testing is often used relatively early in the diagnosis of inborn errors of immunity.
quote: genetics is often used relatively early in diagnosis, compared to other clinical disciplines

fact: Janeway places neutrophil elastase (ELA2) in the azurophilic granules.
quote: encodes neutrophil elastase (ELA2), a component of the azurophilic granules

fact: Janeway states that neutrophil cathelicidin propeptides are stored in secondary granules and are activated by elastase released from primary granules.
quote: the cathelicidin propeptides are stored in the secondary granules... encounter neutrophil elastase that has been released from primary granules

fact: Janeway describes four steps of extravasation: selectin rolling, tight integrin binding, crossing the endothelium and basement membrane, and migration through tissue along chemokine gradients.
quote: The migration of leukocytes out of blood vessels, the process known as extravasation, is thought to occur in four steps.

fact: In CGD, loss of NADPH oxidase activity causes defective superoxide production, so phagocytes fail to kill ingested microbes.
quote: The loss of NADPH oxidase activity results in defective production of superoxide anion... results in a failure to kill phagocytosed microbes.
